🤖 # Job Summary: Aug Hero Run — 535B-A23B MoE (d6144), 18T tokens

Full-scale EP64 MoE pretrain: d6144, **535.3B total / 22.76B active** params, **18.0T tokens** (~**2.70e24** train FLOPs, fwd+bwd), on GB200 with our hand-rolled pooled-wave expert-parallel all-to-all. Data is the two-phase Harrier mixture on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store. Below: model, optimizer, training/topology, the MFU optimizations, the scaling ladder, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters
| | |
|---|---|
| hidden_dim | 6144 |
| num_layers | 48 |
| num_heads | 48 · head_dim 128 |
| num_kv_heads | 12 stored — **local 12 / global 6** (GQA 4:1 local, 8:1 global) |
| num_experts / top-k | **384 / 8** |
| intermediate_dim (expert FFN) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| latent_dim (LatentMoE) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| shared experts | 2 dense SwiGLU, width 3072 |
| vocab_size | 128,256 |
| max_seq_len | 4096 · sliding_window 2048 · global_every 4 |
| capacity_factor / transport cf | 1.15 / 1.15 · num_expert_waves 3 |
| qk_mult | 1.3 · rope θ=10000 (fused, half-RoPE) |
| sconv | sites k/attn/mlp, kernel 4 |
| init | 0.5/√hidden = 0.006379 (uniform, truncated normal) |
| active / total params | 22.76B / 535.3B |

### Features
All structural (always on) unless noted.
- **All-MoE**: every block's MLP is a QB-routed `MoEMLP`; no dense-only layers.
- **GQA, split local/global KV**: sliding-window (local) layers keep 12 KV heads, full-causal (global) layers 6; K/V are sliced/aligned per layer via `lax.cond`, so global layers pay less KV compute.
- **QB routing (histogram estimator)**: router takes top-(K+1) on biased logits; the (K+1)-th logit is the per-token threshold `alpha`, the first K are selected. Each expert's threshold `beta` is the **(1−K/E) upper quantile of the margins `score−alpha`**, read from a **10k-bin histogram over the live global `[min, max]` range** (a `pmin`/`pmax` this step sets the grid; a summed-histogram cumulative count gives the per-expert quantile). The router bias `−beta` is applied on the **next step** as a zero-mean stop-gradient offset — balances expert selection without touching gradients. The histogram estimator is a smoother global quantile than a per-device top-k.
- **Sigmoid combine weights**: combine weights are `sigmoid(unbiased selected logits)`, rescaled so the K weights sum to a fixed 2.5 (not softmax).
- **LatentMoE + learnable latent RMS-norm**: tokens are compressed `hidden→latent (3072)`, passed through a **learnable RMSNorm (`latent_norm`, per-dim gain)** to decouple the expert-input scale from the down-projection init, then dispatched to experts **entirely in latent space**, and projected `latent→hidden` after the weighted combine. The router still reads the full-width token. (Also halves the all-to-all payload — see §4.)
- **Shared experts**: 2 dense SwiGLU experts run on every token in parallel with the routed path; their output is added before the residual.
- **RMSNorm on embeddings and readout**: a learnable-gain [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594) is applied to the token embeddings ([`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223)) and before the untied `lm_head` ([`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1165)), in addition to the per-block `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp`; the GatedNorm below wraps each of these.
- **GatedNorm**: learnable `x·sigmoid(silu(x·w_down)·w_up)` gate (rank-128 bottleneck) applied after **every** RMSNorm (attn, mlp, embed, final).
- **XSA (Exclusive Self-Attention)**: per head, subtract the component of the attention output parallel to its own value vector: `z = y − (yᵀv/‖v‖²)v` — removes the copy-through component so each head learns new information rather than passing V unchanged.
- **Attention head gate**: each head's attention output is scaled by a learned `2·sigmoid(x·attn_gate)`, one scalar per head; `attn_gate` is zero-initialized (gate starts at 1).
- **RMS qk-norm**: Q and K are RMS-normed (non-parametric) per head before RoPE.
- **Partial (half) RoPE, fused**: rotary is applied to **only the first half of head_dim**; the second half is rope-free on every layer. Single-pass fused kernel (θ=10000).
- **Rope-free global layers**: every 4th layer + the last are full-causal and **rope-free** (NoPE, qk_mult-only); the others are sliding-window with RoPE. One per-layer boolean drives mask, KV-head count, and rope together.
- **ShortConv (SConv)**: depthwise causal 1-D conv (kernel 4), identity-init, packed-document segment-masked, at three sites — after K, on the attention-branch output, on the MoE-branch output.
- **Embeddings**: `token_embed` fully replicated + shard-local lookup; `lm_head` (`output_proj`) FSDP+model-sharded; **untied**.
- **Logit z-loss**: the final-logit logsumexp is penalized (`logsumexp_weight = z_loss_weight = 1e-4`) and **added to the training loss** (fused into the CE) — controls gradient-norm growth at long token horizons (the fix the prior scaling ladder surfaced). Distinct from the router z-loss, which is logging-only.
- **Monitoring** (logged, not in loss): per-layer routing entropy, load-balance loss, router z-loss, and sender/receiver token-drop fractions.

## 2. Optimizer — MuonH / AdamH / Adam (compute-scaled)

Three groups via `optax.multi_transform` + a path mask:
- **MuonH** — attention, expert-MLP, shared-expert, latent, and GatedNorm **matrices**. Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (bf16, `backend_steps=5`, quintic coeffs, nesterov momentum 0.95) → **Frobenius-hyperball** scale-invariant step (moves along the direction, projects back onto the param's Frobenius sphere; norms in fp32). Orthogonalization is distributed **intra-rack only** (never crosses DCN); 4D expert stacks are handled without gathering the matrix dims.
- **AdamH** — the **lm_head readout**: Adam moments give the direction, then the same norm-preserving hyperball projection. Gets the MuonH LR, not `adam_lr`.
- **Adam** — `token_embed`, router, router_bias, `attn_gate`, 1-D norm gains, and the tiny SConv kernels.

### Hyperparameters (@ 18T budget)
| | |
|---|---|
| MuonH LR | 0.003291 |
| Adam LR | 0.000759 (MuonH = 13/3 × Adam = 4.33×) |
| beta1 / beta2 | **0.90** / 0.95 |
| epsilon | 6.04e-15 (Adam) · muon_epsilon 1e-8 |
| momentum / nesterov | 0.95 / true |
| use_syrk | true (Blackwell SM100 symmetric GEMM for X·Xᵀ) |
| LR schedule | linear · warmup 1% · min_lr_ratio 0.05 |
| max_grad_norm | none (no global clip) |
| z_loss_weight | 1e-4 (logit z-loss, fused into CE) |

The MuonH/AdamH groups carry **no decoupled weight decay** — they regularize purely through the norm-preserving hyperball projection. LR / beta2 / epsilon are compute-scaled from the Aug hero refit (issues #7856 / #8003, R²=0.978, seq_len=8192): `adam_lr = 0.087571 · tokens^-0.3461 · hidden^-0.3448 · √(tokens_per_batch)`, `beta2 = clip(0.999^(tpb/131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`, `epsilon = 9.676e-18 · √(tokens/tpb)`.

## 3. Training & topology
- **Hardware**: 11× GB200 NVL72 racks. **EP64 within each rack** (expert axis = 16 nodes × 4 GPUs), **data-parallel replication across the 11 racks over DCN**. Mesh `(replica_dcn=11, data, expert=64, model)`; token/batch sharded over `(replica_dcn, data, expert)`.
- **batch_size** 11,264 seqs (1024 × 11 racks) · **seq_len** 4096 · **num_train_steps** 390,139 · **total_tokens 18.0T** · **791 tokens/active-param**.
- **compute_budget** ≈ 2.70e24 FLOPs (analytic, fwd+bwd, latent-corrected).
- **mixed_precision** `params=bf16, compute=bf16, output=bf16`, with **fp32 pinned-host master params** + **offloaded optimizer state** (see §4). Router path kept fp32 before top-k/softmax/QB stats.
- **data**: two-phase Harrier mixture (15T pretrain + 3.75T cooldown, phase-1 at 80% of steps) on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store, marin tokenizer; simulated epoching against the 18.75T reference with a ≤8-epoch cap (max cell exposure ~2.1). 4k-seq pretrain deliberately (2× sequences/batch for expert balancing; token-drop grows sharply at longer context).

## 4. MFU / performance optimizations
- **Hand-rolled fixed pooled-wave all-to-all EP** — every device packs sends into one fixed `[expert_shards, pool_capacity]` pool and receives into fixed per-wave `[local_experts, receiver_cap, H]` buffers; all sizes are compile-time constants so the `all_to_all` runs on fully static shapes. Chosen over `ragged_all_to_all` to avoid a metadata/offset collective and dynamic shapes; **expert IDs ride in-band** as packed header rows in the same activation collective (no separate metadata collective). [EP writeup](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html)
- **Static waves (3)** stripe each destination pool round-robin by rank, shrinking per-wave buffers; each wave is rematerialized to cap activation memory. **Round-robin receiver allocation** keeps overflow drops unbiased across senders.
- **LatentMoE halves EP transport bytes** — the all-to-all carries latent-width (3072) rows both directions instead of hidden (6144). FLOP accounting is corrected for this so MFU isn't overstated.
- **gpu_fa4_cute FA4 attention** — bf16 CuTe segmented flash attention with per-token key lower bounds (no materialized `[B,S,S]` mask, no THD compaction), real GQA, custom CUTLASS backward, grug-tuned 64×64 tiles for B200/head_dim-128. **Sliding-window vs full-causal is just a different lower-bound array feeding the same kernel** → cuts attention FLOPs on the ~3/4 local layers. Bounds are precomputed **outside** the layer scan.
- **Fused linear-softmax cross-entropy (bf16 backward)** — `implementation="xla_fast_bwd"`: streams the whole 65,536-token rank shard over `v_block=4096` vocab blocks with online logsumexp (never materializes the `[B,128k]` logits), and runs both **backward GEMMs in bf16 on tensor cores** (vs fp32/TF32) for ~2.3× on the hero CE shape; the logit z-loss is fused as `logsumexp_weight·lse²`. `v_block=4096` is the dominant MFU lever for the 128k vocab.
- **Fused depthwise causal ShortConv (Pallas)** — the SConv sites dispatch to a fused **Pallas Triton depthwise causal conv** kernel on GPU (forward and `dx` bit-identical to the pad-and-shift reference, `dw` as accurate; pad-and-shift fallback off-GPU). Shard-local (depthwise, no cross-channel/cross-shard term → no collectives); the channel dim is FSDP-sharded so its gradient reduce-scatters.
- **Muon symmetric-GEMM (QuACK SM100) Newton–Schulz** — the two `X·Xᵀ` products in each Newton–Schulz iteration go through a **QuACK symmetric CuTe GEMM** (`use_syrk`) that computes only one triangle of the symmetric output (`A = X·Xᵀ`, then `B = b·A + c·(A·Aᵀ)`) instead of a full dense matmul — roughly halves the matmul FLOPs per iteration on the batched 4D expert stacks, where orthogonalization is the bulk of the optimizer's compute.
- **Padded + resharded distributed Muon (intra-rack)** — the stacked leaves are orthogonalized in parallel across the rack instead of gathered to one device: 3D non-expert stacks **zero-pad the leading (layer) axis** so it divides the intra-rack shard count, then reshard the padded stack over the batch mesh axes (one matrix per shard, `vmap`'d, resliced back after); 4D expert stacks `[layers, experts, fan_in, fan_out]` reshard over the `expert` axis (or the largest batch-axis subset that divides `layers·experts`) and run under a `shard_map` **without ever gathering the `fan_in×fan_out` matrix dims**, then reshard back to the parameter's own spec. All of this is pinned **intra-rack only** — the reshards deliberately exclude the `replica_dcn` axis so Newton–Schulz never runs a collective over the slow inter-rack DCN link.
- **ArrayStacked + `jax.lax.scan`** — all 48 blocks are one compiled body scanned over the layer axis, cutting compile time and HBM; router/QB collectives are structured around the scan.
- **Heterogeneous global/local layers under one homogeneous scan** — `lax.scan` needs a single compiled body, so the ways global (full-causal, rope-free) and local (sliding-window) layers differ can't be Python branches — each rides in as a traced per-layer scalar and is selected *inside* the body:
  - **RoPE diff** — global layers run rope-free. Rather than branch, RoPE is **always computed** and then selected with `jnp.where` on a per-layer `disable_rope` scalar, so both layer kinds compile to the same body.
  - **GQA diff** — local layers keep 12 KV heads, global layers 6. K/V are stored at the max (12) width and sliced-then-`align_kv_heads`'d to the per-layer count via `lax.cond(is_global, …)`, so global layers pay less KV compute without changing the stacked parameter shape.
  - **Mask diff** — the full-causal and sliding-window FA4 bound arrays are precomputed **outside** the scan and the per-layer one is picked with `jnp.where` (the sliding window is a static mask field the body can't vary), so the window rides in as the selected bounds.
- **remat `recompute_all`** — the whole block is recomputed in backward (lowest memory); a `save_moe` mode is available to keep the MoE dispatch tensors and skip re-running the EP collectives.
- **Capacity-factor token dropping (1.15)** bounds expert compute and transport buffers regardless of routing imbalance; drops are counted/logged as sender/receiver fractions.
- **use_syrk** routes the optimizer's `X·Xᵀ` through QuACK's SM100 symmetric GEMM; Newton–Schulz runs in bf16 (halved all-gather bytes) and **intra-rack only**.
- **offload_opt_state + FP32_PINNED_HOST master** — optimizer state and fp32 master weights live in pinned host RAM, shuttled device↔host each step, to leave HBM for the pooled all-to-all buffers. (The pinned-host restore is fixed in [#8443](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8443) and memory-bounded in [#8480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8480); the hero now writes an hourly temporary checkpoint and resumes from it after a preemption.)
- **XLA/runtime flags** — latency-hiding scheduler on, collective-overlap limit 4, CUDA async allocator, 192GB host-memory limit, PGLE off, GPU command buffers disabled.

## 5. Scaling ladder (why, and the rungs)
Runs at 5 widths on one iso-ratio recipe (**791 tokens/active-param**, same mixture + simulated epoching + per-cell epoch structure), ≈1% of total compute, to (a) project performance vs prior recipes and catch bugs, (b) watch grad-norm and token-drop dynamics across scale (the last ladder caught grad-norm growth → the logit z-loss fix), and (c) project evals across the ~100-day trajectory.

| rung | racks | batch | steps | tokens | active |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d768 | 1 | 1024 | 11,420 | 48B | 61M |
| d1024 | 2 | 2048 | 15,276 | 128B | 162M |
| d1536 | 6 | 6144 | 15,128 | 381B | 481M |
| d2048 | 11 | 11,264 | 20,072 | 926B | 1.2B |
| **d6144 (hero)** | 11 | 11,264 | 390,139 | **18.0T** | 22.8B |

## 6. Code (at run commit [`12d8b6f`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be))

**Model** ([`model.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py)) — [`GrugModelConfig`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L160)
- All-MoE routed FFN: [`MoEMLP`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L907) · shared experts [`DenseMLP`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L637)
- QB routing (histogram estimator): threshold/beta [`_qb_beta_hist`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L874), histogram build [`_histogram_from_expert_counts`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L820), applied next-step as stop-grad bias
- Sigmoid combine + renorm-to-2.5: [`_ROUTING_RENORM_SUM`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L58), [combine](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L980)
- LatentMoE + learnable latent RMSNorm: [`latent_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1046)
- RMSNorm on embeddings/readout: [`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223), [`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1203); [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594)
- GatedNorm: [`GatedNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L612)
- XSA (exclusive self-attention): [subtract V-parallel component](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L573)
- Attention head gate (zero-init): [`attn_gate`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L583)
- RMS qk-norm: [`rms_norm(q)`,`rms_norm(k)`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L534)
- Partial (half) RoPE, fused: [`_rope`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L553), [`rope_fused`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L541); rope-free global layers via per-layer bounds [L1252](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1252)
- ShortConv: [`ShortConv`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L420) → fused Pallas [`short_conv`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L52)
- Attention (FA4-cute): [call](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L572), [`fa4_cute_segment_bounds`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1252)
- Untied embeddings: [`token_embed`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1160), [`output_proj`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1163)

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
## Raw Data

On the raw data side, our pool for this hero run is logged at this frozen commit of [our data provenance table on hugging face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/token-counts/commit/3612ddc3350212e38ce8a50b99c3df7ea10b44a9). The raw (pre-dedupe) pool contains 25.6 trillion tokens from 292 sources (though >100 of those are a variety of rollout datasets courtesy of @penfever!).

## Deduplication & Decontamination

For this run, we removed 2.494T tokens through a combination of  fuzzy deduplication and n-gram based decontamination w.r.t many common benchmarks in LM-eval-harness + the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (~250k documents were removed) for a final count of 23.106T tokens. 

Fuzzy duplication used a combination of MinHash deduplication and heuristics among linked pairs within connected component clusters. Examples of duplicates can be found here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/dedup-pair-browser/2026.08.18.2/index.html

## Bucketing

We then embedded all documents with [Harrier 0.6b](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b). 

For topic labels, documents were grouped into 40 semantic buckets by first performing K-means with 5000 clusters (using a sample of 2.56 Million documents) and then doing agglomerative clustering over those 500 clusters to get 40 buckets.

For quality labels, documents were labeled using GLM 5.2 for quality and these labels were distilled into a "Faster Transformer" classifier using both the harrier embedding and the token distribution of the document.

You can see samples from each bucket + distributions from source -> topic x document buckets here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/harrier-k40-cluster-overview/2026.08.18/index.html?revision=uniform-sampling

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: Comparing our scaling law to prior runs. The main differences here is that the May recipe is at compute optimal, this run is at ~12x overtrained, and the 67B-A2B scaling law was at 100x overtrained. The 67B-A2B ran at 8k seqlen, and was therefore given a lower asympotote of 1.4 instead of 1.5. The May fit also inaccurately has an asympotote at 1.6 instead of 1.5. Main architecture change is we dropped from 4/256 level of sparsity to 4/192 level of sparsity (25% fewer total parameters, to fit on GB200 at this scale. Several other small features added. Overall, the scaling law looks reasonable and nothing looks off in the training dynamics or data. Grad norms look stable over the run, peaking at 25% into the run. These runs ran at oversized batch sizes, which may be slightly suppressing the gradient. Expecting the grad norm to climb higher on the hero run, but still peak at the same ~25% into the run. This will be good metric to monitor for issues. Drop rate jumps to 10 pct at very start, then drops to 0, then climbs to ~4pct over the run. Slightly increasing as we scale. Predicting we wont have that 10 percent spike for the hero, because our warmup (1 percent) will cover a much larger number of steps since the hero is at a higher step count. I think most likely scenario is the hero runs around 2 percent dropping, but up to 8 percent seems plausible bsaed on the data at 4k seqlen.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: Also noting- the d2048 scaling ladder rung failed at 81%. Chose not to resume to add more time to Hero Run. The dynamics look clear from the first 81 percent, and we can cleanly extrapolate the last 19%. From a practical perspective, we will not actually be running the end of the run at 4k seqlen, and the datamix may update midrun. So the utility of the scaling law is more around the first 50 percent of the run and ensuring the projection is reasonably within expectation (which it is).

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
From model perspective, main risk points during the run:

1. First 3%. Can we get through LR warmup and reach steady dynamics? If we see gradient run away/large issues here, we likely need to revisit initialization, or potentially initial batch size. Or increase capacity factor if the issue involves high dropping.
2. 30% mark. Gradient may peak, and we will see if gradient keeps climbing, or if its starts to cooldown. Indication that it keeps climbing indefinitely could indicate we need stronger logit z loss, lower token dropping, or revisit some of the norm constraints.
3. Context Extension. How will token dropping respond? See initial Issue desc.
4. Very low loss regime. If training plateaus or acts strange near end of run only, first things to check will be the numerics.

Health checklist:

1. Is total grad norm oscillating steadily? In our May 16B active run, the grad norm grew steadily to 1.5 and training was still very smooth. So I am less concerned with the absolute magnitude, and more concerned with the rate of change. Hyperball makes comparing absolute magnitude not apples to apples with AdamW runs.
2. Are all Hyberball constrained parameters actually respecting the constraint? In past we have seen bug where JAX does norm calculation incorrectly, due to some transient sharding issue. This has been updated to a more explicit calculation that seemed to resolve that issue, but issues of a similar nature may arise.
3. Is token dropping following similar trend as scaling ladder?
4. Is loss decreasing steadily?
5. Are evals decreasing steadily?
6. Is our router bias terms behaving steadily?
7. Does router entropy stay near max?
8. Is embed norm growth reasonable?
9. Is MFU holding constant?
10. Is LR schedule (both Adam and MuonH params) actually following the correct schedule?
11. Does the entire wandb config look accurate?
12. Are we hitting the projected eval targets at each 5 percent?

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
> Thanks for sharing this work. I have a question regarding the motivation behind LatentMoE. Since the training system uses GB200 NVL72 with high-bandwidth NVLink, I am curious why a latent representation is introduced before expert dispatch. Is LatentMoE mainly motivated by reducing communication overhead at larger scales (e.g., beyond a single NVLink domain), or does it also provide benefits beyond communication optimization, such as improving model capability? Thanks!

On its own, LatentMoE halves the comms cost. We found that putting a learnable RMSNorm on the latent projection improved model capability as well, so LatentMoE w/ norm performed better than no latent MoE. Without this learnable RMSNorm, we run into activation scaling issue and see 30 percent worse quality. We also found going from top 4 of 192 to top 8 of 384 (half sized) gave 15 percent quality gain. But it doubles comms cost. So one way to view latentMoE is it enables 4/192->8/384 without change to either comms or compute.

More broadly, do you think dense FFN layers can replace much of the functional role of shared experts? MAI's results suggest that dense layers can carry the common computation while the MoE layers specialize, while also eliminating all-to-all communication on half of the FFN layers. Since the current Hero model uses shared experts partly as a backbone against token dropping, would this design become more attractive once routing is fully dropless?
2. Relative position on local layers + NoPE on global layers.
I also saw the negative Inkling relative-position experiment in #7208. One slightly different variant I'm curious about is using learned relative position only on the sliding-window layers, while leaving global-attention layers completely NoPE. My intuition is that local layers can learn precise relative ordering, while global layers remain position-independent for better long-context extrapolation. Do you think the #7208 result argues against this variant as well, or would it be meaningfully different?
3. AdamH for token embeddings.
In #5203, moving token_embed to AdamH with unit-variance initialization seems to have worked across all four tested scales. However, the current Hero recipe puts token_embed back in Adam. Was that result later invalidated by the MuonH recipe / newer embedding ablations (#6442), or was there another reason it wasn't carried forward?

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: > Thanks for the detailed reply! I have a few follow-up questions after looking through some of the previous Marin experiments. 1. MAI Thinking makes their dense layers only have num_neurons = hidden_dim, which is roughly 3x smaller than normal. This to me a is a bit awkward at first glance because attn is still full capacity every layer. So the normal behavior of attention fetch info, mlp process it is a bit imbalanced (of course if one has data that an idea is good, that it seeming awkward doesn't matter, but it made me more hesitant to spend the time collecting that data instead of working on other things). At very small scale if I do an exact active:total replica (dense 3x width hidden instead of 1x), I get same quality and 20% better MFU than our baseline. But small scale alone is poor signal here, because dense models look much better at small scale in general. We never ended up doing large scale ablation here, since I was more worried about token dropping dynamics. Also the way we are using jax scan makes it a awkward to have different behavior per layer. I am less optimistic about alternating dense/moe long term, because with mature mixture-of-kittens kernels the MFU hit of MoE is probably not that high anyways. 2. Hmm I separately saw some early positive results from Inkling relative position embedding that gave lower loss. But our kernel was not quite fast enough to justify. And perhaps more importantly, the kernel was a bit buggy if I changed sliding window length. I think it should be good on global layers too, since its limited to just the most recent X (512 or 1024) positions. I am more bullish on relative position embedding + MLA. Since MLA has very janky approach to RoPE, which requires replicating 64 head dims across every head. Relative position embedding fixes this. Have to be a bit careful with ablations here because at very small scale RoPE on global looks much better than NoPE on global. (but this fades with scale) 3. So initial AdamH on embed looked good. But later I did learning rate sweep, and if LR was 40% too high, was seeing grad spikes up to 20. I think what was happening (guessing) was rare tokens were having their norm driven to near zero, and then getting massive grad when they finally ended up in the batch. (we have rms_norm on embed that will apply high growth multiplier to small vocab embeds) Dont want any features in the model that require perfectly optimal hypers. So reverted it.

comments.author: MythosAd
comments.body:
Thanks, this is really helpful.

My motivation for alternating dense/MoE is less about the current MFU gap and more about separation of concerns: dense layers handle common computation, while MoE layers handle specialization. Keeping them as two clean execution patterns seems to leave more room for independent kernel, scheduling, and parallelism optimization, even if MoE kernels improve substantially.

For position encoding, my preference for learned relative PE on local layers + NoPE on global layers is mainly to avoid positional extrapolation entirely. With a fixed local window, the relative-position range never changes as context grows, while global attention stays purely content-addressed. I agree this probably needs larger-scale ablations to judge properly.

issues.body:
**TL;DR.** We ran the Snowball E11 RL regimen against `Qwen/Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507` to check whether the SkyRL/Iris training path holds at 235B on a third-party MoE. It does: six full optimizer steps on 96 H100s with no OOM, no rank drop, no NCCL abort, and importance-sampling ratios that stayed at 1.000. The run produced no learning signal, and we stopped it at step 6 of 50. The cause was a generation budget sized for a different model — 55% of samples hit the 8,192-token cap instead of finishing — so the objective was dominated by a truncation penalty rather than by correctness. Steps took ~9 hours each, 3× our pre-registered throughput limit.

## Setup

Port of the E11 regimen (DeepScaleR, 39,304 rows; `aime` verifier; batch 256 × 16 samples; 10,240-token window = 2,048 input + 8,192 generation; DAPO clip 0.2/0.4 with the dynamic-sampling filter; TIS cap 2.0) from Marin's 67B-A2B Grug to `Qwen/Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507` @ `6cbffae6`. Run `rl-qwen3-235b-a22b-thinking-2507-rno2a-d-20260822-140923-13aad3`, launched 2026-08-22 14:09 UTC.

Geometry: 12 × H100x8 = 96 GPUs — 8 policy nodes (FSDP2, EP 1, `cpu_offload` on) and 4 inference engines at TP 8. Weights staged from an in-region S3 mirror, 118 safetensors, 438 GB.

## What held up

The stack ran a 235B third-party MoE end to end. Each risk we wrote down before launching came back clean on the systems side:

- No OOM at init or in any backward pass, on 64 GPUs with `cpu_offload`.
- No runaway dynamic-sampling discard; generation completed every step and never hit the `max_sample_batches` stop.
- TIS agreed closely between trainer and vLLM: `imp_ratio_mean` 1.000, `|log r|` 0.043, token `|Δlog p|` μ/p99 0.0139 / 0.128.
- Checkpoint volume stayed inside its budget at 4.8 TiB across 601 objects on a TTL prefix.

We had not previously trained a model this size, or a non-Marin MoE, on this path. That part of the question is answered.

## Timings

From the driver log, per-step wall-clock:

| step | logged (UTC) | Δ |
| ---: | --- | ---: |
| 1 | 08-23 00:30:59 | 10 h 22 m from submit (incl. bring-up and the streamed 438 GB EP load) |
| 2 | 08-23 09:32:34 | 9 h 02 m |
| 3 | 08-23 18:24:53 | 8 h 52 m |
| 4 | 08-24 03:32:10 | 9 h 07 m |
| 5 | 08-24 12:41:44 | 9 h 09 m |
| 6 | 08-24 21:40:08 | 8 h 58 m |

~9 hours per step, σ ≈ 7 minutes across the five intervals. Bring-up to first step-1 metrics was 10 h 22 m, of which about 1 h 20 m is scheduling plus the expert-parallel load and the rest is the step itself.

Six steps cost 59.6 hours on 96 GPUs, roughly 5,700 GPU-hours. The 50-step horizon would have run ~19 days holding 19% of the cluster. We had set `> 3 h/step` as the line where throughput becomes the problem.

## Why there was no learning signal

| step | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `environment/acc` | 0.3218 | 0.3381 | 0.2805 | 0.3193 | 0.2805 | 0.3167 |
| `reward/avg_raw_reward` | −0.049 | −0.145 | −0.011 | −0.039 | −0.138 | −0.084 |
| `policy/policy_entropy` | 0.1080 | 0.1066 | 0.1061 | 0.1061 | 0.1072 | 0.1071 |

Accuracy oscillates in a 0.28–0.34 band with no direction, reward is flat to slightly negative, and entropy is flat to three decimals. `avg_pass_at_16` reads 1.0000 at every step, but that is measured after the dynamic-sampling filter has dropped uninformative groups, so it carries no signal here.

At step 6, `stop_reason/length` was 2,241 against `stop_reason/stop` 1,855 out of 4,096 samples: 54.7% of generations never terminated, with mean response length 6,282 tokens against the 8,192 cap. Non-termination rose from 0.491 at the first read to 0.547; we had set 0.3 as the gate.

That is the whole result. More than half of every batch was scored on a truncation penalty instead of on whether the answer was right, so the gradient was mostly about length. It also explains the step time: over half the samples ran to the cap, paying full generation cost and returning nothing usable.

The mismatch is structural. `Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507` emits long chain-of-thought by design, and we gave it a window sized for a 67B-A2B model. Both available fixes cost more than this arm was worth: a larger generation budget makes a 9-hour step longer, and turning thinking off trains something other than the model we wanted to evaluate.

## Where we landed

Stopped at step 6 by owner decision. No checkpoint was exported and no held-out evaluation was run, so there is no model artifact or downstream score to report. Logs, traces, trajectories, and the resolved config are preserved; the run's S3 prefixes have been deleted.

If we come back to this: size the window to the model instead of inheriting it from the previous experiment. A thinking variant needs a budget above its natural trace length — 16k or more, given a 6.3k mean while truncated — which at this geometry means accepting a step time well past 9 hours, or a smaller model, or more inference engines. Both gates we set beforehand fired at step 1; we should have acted on them then rather than at step 6.

Recorded here for the negative result and the timing numbers; reopen if the window-sizing follow-up is picked up.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Just kicking off: measure whether adaptive environment/problem sampling improves RL training efficiency under a fixed compute budget, versus uniform random sampling.

## Description

We run SkyRL GRPO post-training on a small Qwen policy (0.6B class) over a pool of verifiable, non-agentic environments (math datasets spanning difficulty, plus simple programmatic tasks). Each arm uses the same model, data pool, and budget; only the policy for choosing which environment/problem to roll out next differs.

Arms:

1. Naive sampling: uniform random over the pool (baseline).
2. Modified Thompson sampling: bias toward environments currently yielding reward signal (e.g. per-env reward variance / pass-rate entropy), with decay so the belief tracks policy drift.
3. Pre-graded difficulty (problems graded 0–N easiest→hardest):
   - Naive curriculum: 1/N of budget per level.
   - Adaptive curriculum: train on a level until it stops paying (saturated or not learning), then move.
   - Biased sampling: grades seed an initial belief distribution for the Thompson sampler.

Budget: fixed output-token count per run, falling back to GPU wall-time (64 H100s x fixed hours) if token accounting is impractical. Runs use INTERACTIVE priority on cw-rno2a. The experiment is wired through Marin artifact steps (`marin.rl.skyrl`) so arms are cached and rerunnable; sampler support lands on a MarinSkyRL branch if the pinned trainer lacks the hooks.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Reward-signal-aware sampling concentrates rollouts where the learning signal is, so adaptive arms should reach a given eval score with fewer output tokens than uniform sampling. Quantify the value of each mechanism at fixed budget.

## Status

Kickoff. Wiring the experiment directory and a small smoke run.

Planned milestones, posted as comments:

1. Initial smoke run working end to end.
2. Curriculum/sampling infrastructure wired.
3. Results per sampling arm.
4. Final report on arm efficacy and follow-up recommendations.

## Links

* Logbook:
* W&B Report:
* Important updates:

## Decision Log

## Conclusion

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Wiring status: the training loop works end to end; the smoke milestone is blocked only on a MarinSkyRL export bug.

What ran: `experiments/post_training/curriculum_rl/` builds a 6-bin graded pool (GSM8K, MATH L1-2/3/4/5, AIME 1983-2024; 10,427 train rows, 756 validation rows), mirrors Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B@c1899de, and runs SkyRL GRPO on 2 nodes of cw-rno2a H100s at interactive priority through `skyrl_step`, with pool/model artifacts cached across attempts. The smoke run completed all 4 GRPO steps over the mixed-env parquet (per-row `env_class`), logging per-environment metrics (train `environment/acc` 0.023 at step 4 — the raw 0.6B policy under a 1024-token cap).

Fixes landed on the branch along the way:

1. MarinSkyRL pin b45a6ed2 crashed at startup (`SKYRL_DEBUG_ARTIFACT_DIR is required`); advanced to d018d672, which contains the upstream fix.
2. The `aime` env asserts `extras["reward_model"]["ground_truth"]` (the gsm8k env reads `reward_spec`); pool rows now carry both columns.
3. The `aime` env verifies with the Minerva `Answer: ...` extraction, not `\boxed{}`; prompts now elicit a final Answer line. Representative ground truths (integers, degrees, fractions, tuples, radicals, polynomials) pass the skyrl-gym contract's two-sided preflight.

Open blocker: at d018d672 the terminal policy export (`cloud.iris.export_hf_checkpoint`) dies with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'torch'` — `skyrl_train/hf_export.py` pulls `skyrl_train.utils`, whose package init imports torch, into the deliberately torch-free launcher env. comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Milestone 2: infrastructure wired for curricula & sampling.**

The curriculum sampler is implemented on MarinSkyRL branch [`curriculum-sampling`](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/tree/curriculum-sampling) (@2a9034fd) and validated live: naive, thompson, and grade-adaptive smoke arms all ran green end-to-end (train → HF export → eval) on cw-rno2a.

Design: a `data.sampling` config subtree selects a stateful weighted sampler over the pool's graded bins (`extra_info.data_source` / `grade`). Kinds: `naive` (stock shuffle), `thompson` (Beta posterior on the decay-weighted fraction of *informative* GRPO groups — groups whose rollout rewards are not all equal), `grade-uniform` (equal budget per grade), `grade-adaptive` (train one grade until its informative fraction stays below a threshold for a window, then advance), `grade-prior` (Thompson seeded with grade-derived optimism). The sampler is checkpoint-resumable (torchdata Stateful) and rejects duplicate rows per batch to preserve the GRPO group invariant.

Smoke evidence the machinery works (4-step runs, Qwen3-0.6B, non-thinking):
- thompson: weights collapsed to ~1% on the two bins with zero informative groups (MATH-L5, AIME) and concentrated on informative middle bins.
- grade-adaptive: 80% mass on grade 0 (gsm8k, informative_frac 0.47 — not yet exhausted, level correctly held at 0) with 20% exploration.
- Non-thinking mode fixed the truncation problem: 85% → 20% truncated, 4% → 70% parseable answers, ~500 avg output tokens.

Fixes along the way: unstepped-episode metrics crash, over-length prompts filtered at pool build (8 rows dropped), per-token reward scalarization for the sampler, batch-unique draws.

Next: full-scale arms (64 GPUs, 120 steps × 512 prompts × 8 samples each) starting with the naive baseline.

Base non-thinking Qwen3-0.6B started near val-math500 ≈ 0 and gsm8k ≈ 0.65, so every arm learns substantially. Wall time was ~1.75h for every arm (generation runs on fixed engine capacity), so fixed-step is also approximately fixed-GPU-hours: 5 arms × 64 GPU × 1.75h.

Reading: curriculum arms buy **token efficiency, not a better endpoint at equal steps**. grade-adaptive matched or beat the mid-run baselines while generating 53% of naive's tokens (it trains mostly on easier, shorter problems until they stop being informative); thompson tracks close behind and reallocates automatically without pre-grading. Final report with recommendations follows.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Final report: efficacy and recommendations.**

**Conclusions.**
1. *Curriculum value here is token efficiency, not a better endpoint.* At a fixed generated-token budget (146M), grade-adaptive reached mid-run-baseline quality at ~53% of naive's token spend (val-math500 0.156 vs 0.080), with thompson close behind (0.140). At a fixed step/GPU-hour budget — where generation capacity is already paid for — naive was the best MATH500 arm (0.460) and thompson the best gsm8k arm (0.516); no curriculum dominated naive.
2. *Thompson sampling is the best no-prep default.* No offline grading required, decay handles policy drift, competitive under both budget definitions, and it visibly reallocated: bins with zero informative groups (MATH L5, AIME — all-fail for a 0.6B policy) dropped to the 1% floor.
3. *Grade-prior and grade-uniform added little* — the grade-derived prior washes out once real reward evidence accumulates, and fixed 1/N allocation wastes budget on uninformative extremes.

**Recommendations.**
- Re-run naive / thompson / grade-adaptive at 3 seeds for error bars before production conclusions (~$3 × current spend; each arm is 64 GPUs × 1.75 h).
- Extend grade-adaptive to 300+ steps so it traverses all grades; its curve was still rising at half the token budget.
- Make thompson difficulty-directional (distinguish all-pass from all-fail groups) — that should recover grade-adaptive's token efficiency without pre-grading.
- Batch-level uninformative-group resampling (DAPO-style) is complementary to bin-level sampling and likely stacks.

**Artifacts.** Sampler: MarinSkyRL `curriculum-sampling` @ 2a9034fd (checkpoint-resumable `data.sampling` subtree; worth PRing to main after multi-seed validation). Experiment: `experiments/post_training/curriculum_rl/` (PR to follow). Runs and curves: W&B project `marin-community/marin-curriculum-rl`; exported checkpoints under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/power/checkpoints/curriculum-rl/<arm>/2026.08.29/exports/global_step_120`.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Round 2 starting.** Scope, per review of round-1 results:

1. **DAPO dynamic sampling** — the pinned trainer already ships `trainer.algorithm.dynamic_sampling` (filter/replace with cross-batch accumulation); wiring it as arm variants (naive+dapo, thompson+dapo). One fix needed first: the curriculum-stat update must run before the filter, or every bin looks 100% informative to the sampler.
2. **Prior-sensitive pool** — round 1's grade-prior collapsed to thompson because 120 steps × 512 prompts of reward evidence swamps any prior over just 6 bins. Adding procedurally generated reasoning-gym bins (arithmetic chains, etc.) whose difficulty knobs give *genuine a-priori grades* and widen the bin count, so priors have room to matter. The reasoning-gym scorers only award 1.0 for a bare exact answer (full CoT responses get length-fuzz partial credit), so the env gets Minerva-style `Answer:`-line extraction first.
3. **Directional sampler** — new `learnability` kind: Thompson on per-bin pass rate, weight ∝ sampled p(1−p), which peaks at 50% solve rate and down-weights both all-pass and all-fail bins directionally (round-1 thompson treated them identically). `grade-prior` v2 seeds this posterior with grade-decreasing prior pass rates, so the prior is used directionally instead of as undirected optimism.
4. **Dropped:** grade-uniform (no signal over its simpler relatives in round 1).

Round-2 arms: naive, thompson, learnability, grade-prior(directional), grade-adaptive, naive+dapo, thompson+dapo — same fixed budgets and eval protocol as round 1.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Round 2 infrastructure wired; smoke green.** All four follow-ups are implemented and validated end-to-end on cw-rno2a (`/power/curriculum-rl-r2-smoke2`):

- **DAPO** — `trainer.algorithm.dynamic_sampling.type=filter` wired as arm variants `naive-dapo` / `thompson-dapo`. The curriculum sampler now updates on **raw pre-filter batches** (MarinSkyRL `9a7286b4`); previously it would have run post-filter and read every bin as 100% informative. Smoke shows the filter engaging: 33–50/64 prompts informative per raw batch, one resample batch per step.
- **Prior-sensitive datasets** — pool v3 adds seven procedurally generated reasoning-gym bins (chain_sum ×3, spell_backward ×2, base_conversion ×2; 1,200 rows each) whose difficulty knobs give genuine a-priori grades, interleaved with the re-graded math bins on a shared 0–10 scale. The `reasoning_gym` env scores only the final `Answer:` line (`d36ceaaa`) — full CoT responses previously got ~0.05 fuzz credit even when correct. Smoke pass rates confirm the machinery and expose grade-placement surprises to analyze at full scale (chain_sum-med ~0.9 at grade 3; spell-backward ~0.15–0.33 vs math-l12 ~0.03 — spelling is easier for the base model than its grade assumed).
- **Directional sampler** — new `learnability` kind: Thompson draw on each bin's decayed pass rate, weighted by p·(1−p), peaking at 50% solve rate so it distinguishes too-easy from too-hard (the informative-group signal alone cannot). `grade-prior` is redefined as its grade-seeded variant: prior pass-rate mean falls linearly from 0.85 (easiest grade) to 0.05 (hardest) with pseudo-count `grade_prior_strength` (`0b44138c`).
- **Grade-uniform dropped** from the arm catalog.

Launching round-2 full arms next: naive, thompson, learnability, grade-adaptive, grade-prior, naive-dapo, thompson-dapo — 120 steps × 64 H100s each on the expanded pool.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 # Round 2 final report: DAPO, procedural bins, and directional samplers

All seven arms completed: 120 GRPO steps each on 64 H100s (cw-rno2a, Qwen3-0.6B, batch 512×8 samples, non-thinking, ~1024-token generations). Every arm shares the same expanded pool and differs only in prompt sampling and (for the DAPO variants) group filtering. Terminal evals are Evalchemy MATH500 and GSM8K-0shot against the exported step-120 checkpoint; in-run validation is scored by the training environments on held-out slices.

## Results

| arm | generated tokens | in-run val (all) | MATH500 | GSM8K-0shot |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| naive | 203M | 0.513 | 0.362 | 0.390 |
| thompson | 149M | 0.480 | 0.350 | 0.409 |
| learnability | 220M | 0.537 | 0.418 | 0.444 |
| grade-adaptive | 130M | 0.534 | 0.346 | 0.439 |
| grade-prior (directional) | 211M | 0.487 | 0.408 | 0.418 |
| naive-dapo | 190M | 0.555 | 0.414 | 0.401 |
| **thompson-dapo** | 205M | **0.571** | **0.434** | **0.456** |

Token totals include work redone after preemption-driven restarts (real spend). Round-2 numbers are not comparable to round 1: the pool now spends a large share of budget on procedural bins, which lowers math transfer for every arm equally (round-1 naive hit 0.460 MATH500 on the math-only pool).

![score vs tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r2/all-tokens.png)
![score vs steps](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r2/all-steps.png)

MATH500 and GSM8K validation trajectories against token spend:

![val-math500 vs tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r2/val-math500-tokens.png)
![val-gsm8k vs tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r2/val-gsm8k-tokens.png)

## Grading mechanism and distributions

Grades place all 13 bins on one 0–10 scale from two sources. Math bins take grades from **source metadata**: GSM8K at 1, MATH levels 1–2/3/4/5 at 2/4/6/8, AIME at 10. Procedural reasoning-gym bins take **a-priori grades from generator knobs**, assigned before any model saw a sample: chain_sum at grades 0/3/7 (2 terms 1–2 digits → 5–6 terms 4 digits signed), spell_backward at 5/9 (3–5 vs 8–10 letters), base_conversion at 5/9 (bases 2–10 values ≤500 vs bases 11–16). Train pool: 18,619 rows (gsm8k 2000, math-l12 1911, math-l3 1590, math-l4 1690, math-l5 2296, aime 932, 7 procedural bins × 1200); validation adds 128-row held-out generator draws per procedural family.

How well did the grades predict reality? Realized pass rates from the learnability arm:

| bin (grade) | pass rate @ step 10 | @ step 120 |
|---|---|---|
| rg-sum-easy (0) | 0.97 | 1.00 |
| gsm8k (1) | 0.49 | 0.84 |
| math-l12 (2) | 0.53 | 0.84 |
| rg-sum-med (3) | 0.97 | 0.99 |
| math-l3 (4) | 0.41 | 0.70 |
| rg-spell-short (5) | 0.82 | 1.00 |
| rg-base-small (5) | 0.58 | 0.90 |
| math-l4 (6) | 0.28 | 0.57 |
| rg-sum-hard (7) | 0.74 | 0.90 |
| math-l5 (8) | 0.07 | 0.27 |
| rg-base-large (9) | 0.26 | 0.96 |
| rg-spell-long (9) | 0.79 | 0.97 |
| aime (10) | 0.00 | 0.06 |

Two clear findings. **Within a family, metadata grades rank difficulty essentially perfectly** (math: 0.53 → 0.41 → 0.28 → 0.07 → 0.004 down the levels). **Across families, knob-derived grades misjudged absolute difficulty badly**: arithmetic chains are near-trivial for Qwen3-0.6B at any knob setting we chose, and spelling/base-conversion saturate within ~10 steps once the model learns the answer format — procedural tasks measure format acquisition more than reasoning. The pre-registered grades were wrong in exactly the way a real practitioner's would be, which made this a fair test of whether samplers recover from miscalibrated priors.

## Sampling mechanisms

- **naive** — the stock uniform shuffle without replacement. Control.
- **thompson** — Beta Thompson sampling on each bin's decayed *informative-group fraction* (a GRPO group is informative when its rewards are not all equal), decay 0.95, 5% probability floor. Round 1's design.
- **learnability** (new) — Thompson draw on each bin's decayed per-sample *pass rate*, weighted by p·(1−p), which peaks at 50% solve rate. Motivated by round 1's core diagnosis: informative-fraction cannot distinguish a too-easy bin from a too-hard one (both produce uniform groups), so it has no direction.
- **grade-prior** (redesigned) — learnability with grade-seeded Beta priors: prior mean pass rate falls linearly from 0.85 at the easiest grade to 0.05 at the hardest, with 8 pseudo-counts. Round 1's undirected-optimism version collapsed to thompson within ~20 steps; this version encodes the grade as a belief about *pass rate*, which the p·(1−p) weighting turns into "start in the middle band."
- **grade-adaptive** — a level pointer walking the grade ladder, advancing when the current level stops producing informative signal; 20% exploration mass off-level.
- **DAPO filter** (`naive-dapo`, `thompson-dapo`) — drop zero-advantage groups after generation and keep drawing batches until a full informative batch accumulates (the standard DAPO dynamic-sampling recipe). The curriculum sampler updates on raw pre-filter batches so filtering does not bias its statistics.

Weight trajectories show the directional machinery working as designed. Learnability zeroes the saturated procedural bins almost immediately, holds AIME near the floor, and walks its mass up the math ladder as the model improves (math-l3/l4 dominate late). Grade-prior starts mid-band per its prior, then evidence overrides the miscalibrated procedural placements within ~15 steps:

![learnability weights](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r2/curriculum-learnability-weight.png)
![grade-prior weights](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r2/curriculum-grade-prior-weight.png)

## Analysis

1. **DAPO is the single biggest win.** thompson-dapo leads every metric, and both DAPO arms beat their non-DAPO counterparts at *equal token spend*, not just equal steps — filtering converts budget that would fund zero-gradient groups into informative ones. The score-vs-tokens chart shows the DAPO curves rising fastest through the whole budget range.
2. **Direction matters more than curriculum-ness.** Learnability (0.418/0.444) beats thompson (0.350/0.409) decisively — same Thompson machinery, better signal. Plain thompson was the weakest arm, confirming round 1's suspicion that informative-fraction is a compass without a needle.
3. **Grades survive contact with reality only where they were right.** Grade-prior recovered from its miscalibrated procedural priors but paid an early-budget tax for them, landing between thompson and learnability. With honest grades (the math family) the ordering is genuinely useful; with guessed grades the evidence-driven samplers simply relearn the truth and the prior contributes little. Grading effort is only worth what the grader knows.
4. **Grade-adaptive remains the token-efficiency champion** (0.534 val-all on 130M tokens, ~64% of naive's spend), echoing round 1. Its focused single-level sampling generates shorter, more solvable rollouts.
5. **Procedural tasks are cheap curriculum filler but weak transfer vehicles.** They gave the samplers real difficulty structure to exploit and clean val curves (e.g. base-conversion 0.26→0.96), but every arm's MATH500 dropped versus round 1's math-only pool. At 0.6B, budget spent on spelling does not buy math.

## Conclusions and future work

At fixed budget, the value ranking is: DAPO filtering > directional (pass-rate) sampling > adaptive level curricula > grade priors > informative-fraction sampling. The obvious composition — **learnability + DAPO** — was not run this round and is the first follow-up: the mechanisms are orthogonal (what to sample vs what to keep) and their gains plausibly stack.

Future work, in priority order:
- **learnability-dapo arm** at the same budget point.
- **Measured grades over guessed grades**: a ~1-hour pre-pass scoring k samples per bin with the base model would have produced a nearly perfect prior for free; grade-prior with measured priors is the honest test of "grades as belief."
- **Token-budget-equalized stopping** (stop every arm at, say, 150M generated tokens) to remove the step/token conflation entirely.
- **A model one size up** (4–8B, thinking mode) where AIME-band bins are learnable and the grade ladder has more headroom.
- Infra hardening from this round is tracked separately: #8774 (gang restart after head preemption, in progress), #8781/#8782 (TAS priority preemption, merged), plus the eval endpoint queue-time fix and TTL-routed Ray session logs in #8769.

Experiment code and pins are in #8769 (`experiments/post_training/curriculum_rl/`, MarinSkyRL `curriculum-sampling` @ `4a1f99fc`). Charts regenerate with `report_charts.py`; per-bin stats with `report_pool_stats.py`; terminal scores with `report_evals.py`.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Round-3 finding: adaptive sampling is fragile to reward-contract mismatch; grade priors buy robustness.

The snowball-learnability-dapo arm showed val-gsm8k pass@1 = 0.000 at step 10 while snowball-naive scored 0.891 from the same base model — with learnability simultaneously beating naive on harder bins (MATH-500 0.66 vs 0.63). Retained trajectories pin the cause: Snowball answers gsm8k correctly but in its SFT style (`\boxed{300}`), while the gsm8k environment's rule grader only accepts the answer after `"####"`, so every rollout scores 0. The bin's zero pass rate measures format compliance, not ability.

The three samplers then diverge exactly along their designs:

- **naive** samples gsm8k uniformly (~54 rollouts/step); rare rollouts that happen to emit `####` get positive advantage and RL teaches the format within 10 steps → val 0.891.
- **learnability + group-informative weighting** observes pass = 0 at step 1, assigns the bin near-floor weight (0.009 vs ~0.09 for active bins), starves it, and never learns the format → val 0.000.
- **grade-prior + group-informative** keeps sampling on its grade-3 prior (9 informative groups by step 9, pass EMA 0.16 → 0.33) and recovers → val 0.828 at step 10.

Letting the arms run to 60 steps as-is: the dynamics are the experiment. For the report, the snowball headline metric will be shown with and without val-gsm8k, since the bin conflates format with difficulty for this model. Follow-up recommendation: normalize every pool bin to one answer contract (`\boxed{}` + math-verify) so grades measure difficulty only, and add cold-start optimism or a re-exploration floor to pure-feedback samplers so an observed-zero bin is revisited often enough to distinguish "too hard" from "mis-specified".

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Round-3 final report: graded-ladder curricula on Qwen3-0.6B and Snowball 67B-A2B.

All nine arms completed: six Qwen arms (120 steps, 64 H100s each, ~230–247M generated tokens) and three Snowball arms (60 steps, 64 H100s each, ~64–75M tokens) on the grade 0–13 math ladder, scored by the fixed end metric (validation pass@1 weighted by 1+grade, never visible to samplers).

| arm | grade-weighted | without gsm8k | frontier grade | tokens |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| qwen learnability-dapo | **0.312** | 0.266 | 9 | 247M |
| snowball grade-prior-dapo | **0.310** | 0.256 | **13** | 71M |
| qwen grade-prior-dapo | 0.301 | 0.255 | 9 | 245M |
| qwen naive-dapo | 0.294 | 0.248 | 5 | 229M |
| snowball naive | 0.289 | 0.232 | 5 | 64M |
| qwen grade-prior | 0.283 | 0.238 | 5 | 240M |
| qwen naive | 0.267 | 0.219 | 5 | 231M |
| qwen grade-adaptive | 0.257 | 0.211 | 5 | 144M |
| snowball learnability-dapo | 0.166 | 0.181 | 5 | 75M |

![grade-weighted score vs tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r3/grade-weighted-tokens.png)

**Qwen: curriculum sampling wins cleanly.** Both group-informative curriculum arms beat plain DAPO, which beats everything else: learnability-dapo ends +17% relative over naive (0.312 vs 0.267) and +6% over naive-dapo. Only the two curriculum-DAPO arms pushed the frontier to grade 9 (AMC pass@1 ≥ 0.25); every other arm stalled at grade 5 (MATH). Grade-adaptive (ladder-walking) finished last and also spent the fewest tokens — it parks on easy bins with short responses.

![frontier grade vs tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r3/frontier-grade-tokens.png)

**Snowball: grade priors won; pure feedback-driven sampling failed twice.** grade-prior-dapo reached 0.310 with frontier grade 13 (TheoremQA ≥ 0.25) in 71M tokens and was still improving at step 60. The learnability arm hit both failure modes:

1. *Format-contract starvation* (details in the [mid-run comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8765#issuecomment-5471696465)): gsm8k pass@1 stayed 0.000 for the entire run because an observed zero pass rate zeroes the group-informative weight; naive learned the `####` contract by step 10 (0.94 final) and grade-prior recovered through its prior (0.95 final).
2. *Late-run collapse*: stable through step 50 (MATH-500 0.64–0.70, TheoremQA 0.25–0.28), then one destabilizing update at step 60 — raw grad-norm 19,332, KL-max 9.3, entropy 0.085 — dropped every bin (MATH-500 → 0.52), and the terminal export captured the damaged checkpoint. Snowball-naive also slid from its 0.324 mid-run peak to 0.289; only grade-prior-dapo ended at its peak. Single-seed caveat applies, but concentrated sampling appears to raise late-run variance.

![val-gsm8k vs tokens](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r3/val-gsm8k-tokens.png)

**The sampling objective checks out empirically.** Pooling per-bin pass-rate transitions across all curriculum arms, learning velocity peaks near pass rate 0.4–0.5 (~0.008/step) and falls to ~0 at both extremes — matching the flat-topped group-informative curve 1−pⁿ−(1−p)ⁿ more closely than p(1−p):

![learning velocity vs pass rate](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/assets/curriculum-rl-r3/velocity-vs-pass-rate.png)

**Infrastructure notes.** Snowball steps ran at ~8.8 min after raising `micro_train_batch_size_per_gpu` 1→4 (the FSDP update was all-gather-bound: 32 sequential re-gathers of 134GB shards for ~2B active params of compute; the fix cut policy_train 1660s→437s). Remaining round-3 ops incidents were all transient: one driver OOM at the default 1GB coordinator memory, one eval endpoint-registration timeout, one export stuck on an Iris pod race after its container completed.

**Recommendations for a round 4.**
- Normalize every bin to one answer contract (`\boxed{}` + math-verify) so grades measure difficulty, not instruction-style compliance.
- Give pure-feedback samplers cold-start optimism and a re-exploration floor that periodically re-probes zero-pass bins; without it they cannot distinguish "too hard" from "mis-specified".
- Default to grade priors when moving a curriculum to a new model: they were never worse than naive on any bin, on either model.
- Add a stability guard (KL trust region or late LR decay) for long runs under concentrated sampling; the step-60 blowup was visible in grad-norm before the eval caught it.

Full chart set and summary.json: [assets/curriculum-rl-r3](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/assets/curriculum-rl-r3).

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Round 4 launched: `/power/curriculum-r4-full` on cw-us-east-02a — Snowball, `naive` vs `grade-prior-dapo`, 120 steps at pool version `2026.09.01.1`.

Changes from round 3:

- **Optimizer**: MuonH at lr 1e-5, weight_decay 0, grad clip 1.0 — the same recipe Snowball pretrained/SFT'd with. Round 3 used AdamW at 2e-6.
- **Batch shape**: 64 prompts × 8 samples × 120 steps (same rollout total as round 3's 60 bigger steps, 2× fresher policy), micro-batch 8 — halves the all-gather count that dominated round-3 step time.
- **Prompt contracts**: system prompt plus strengthened per-bin format instructions baked into the pool. Served-model A/B (temp 1.0, rule-graded, 100 problems/variant): gsm8k 0.00 → 0.55 and math500 0.05 → 0.15 before any RL; failures under the old prompts were correct math ending in `\boxed{}` instead of the graded answer line.
- **Curriculum**: the grade-prior-dapo arm adds `reversion_mass=2.0` — per-step pseudo-evidence that pulls starved bins back toward re-probeable weight, addressing the round-3 starvation self-lock (MarinSkyRL `129ed37a`).

Smoke (4 steps, MuonH + micro=8): step time 222s vs 534s in round 3, raw grad norm 0.38–0.47 under the 1.0 clip. At 222s/step the full arms should take ~7.5h each.

Next: monitor both arms to completion, verify think-token structure and truncation rates from retained trajectories, then the round-4 report.

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 Round 4 complete. Both Snowball arms ran 120 steps at `2026.09.01.1` (MuonH lr 1e-5, system prompt + strengthened format contracts, `reversion_mass=2.0` on the curriculum arm). The grade-prior-dapo arm finished in one attempt; naive hit two micro-batch-8 CUDA OOMs (steps 92 and 119) and resumed cleanly from checkpoint both times.

Final evals (round-3 in parentheses):

| arm | grade-weighted | frontier grade | metered tokens |
|---|---|---|---|
| naive | 0.285 (0.289) | 5 (5) | 89M |
| grade-prior-dapo | **0.292** (0.310) | **13** (13) | 81M |

Headlines:

- The prompt contract moved the format unlock out of RL: both arms hit val-gsm8k ≥ 0.89 at the first eval (step 10), and the naive-vs-curriculum composite gap shrank from +0.021 to +0.007. Most of round 3's curriculum margin was exposure to a format-deceptive bin; a two-paragraph prompt buys the same thing.
- The frontier edge is what survives: grade-prior-dapo again sustained the grade-13 bin (theoremqa 0.268, crossing ~75M tokens) while naive never did — the same 13-vs-5 split as round 3 under a different optimizer, batch shape, and prompt.
- MuonH at 5× the round-3 lr was stable end to end (grad norms 0.17–0.47 under the 1.0 clip, no late-run collapse), and micro-batch 8 halved step time (222s vs 534s).
- `reversion_mass` behaved as designed: all 19 bin weights stayed within a ~3× band; no floor-lock.
- Regression: peak val-math500 fell 0.656 → 0.562 in both arms (candidates: 512 vs 1024 rollouts/step, lr drift, or the anti-`\boxed{}` contract; unresolved at one seed).
- Retained-trajectory analysis: 40–48% of rollouts still hit the 2048-token cap at end of training; frontier bins truncate near-totally (AIME 98%, Omni 99%). Successful rollouts are short, ~100% think-token structured by step 100, and `\boxed{}` was ground out of successes entirely. Generation budget, not sampling, is now the binding constraint — top round-5 lever.

Paper (round-4 section added) and all figures: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/assets/curriculum-rl-paper/paper.md

comments.author: rjpower
comments.body:
🤖 **Round 5 launched** (`/power/curriculum-r5-full`, version `2026.09.02.1`): naive + grade-prior-dapo, 120 steps × 64 prompts × 8 samples, with the round-4 recipe (MuonH 1e-5, clip 1.0, reversion_mass 2.0) and two changes:

- **Generation budget 2048 → 8192** (window 9216, same 1024-token prompt budget). Round 4's binding constraint: 40–48% of rollouts truncated at the cap, AIME/Omni/TheoremQA near-totally. `micro_train_batch_size_per_gpu` 8 → 2 to hold activation memory at the longer sequences.
- **System prompt 111 → 37 tokens.** Served-model A/B (temp 1.0, rule-graded, 100–250 rows/variant, strong per-bin suffixes held fixed):

  | system prompt | gsm8k comp/pass | math500 comp/pass | theoremqa comp/pass |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | current 111t | 0.79/0.38 | 0.60/0.16 | 0.42/0.04 |
  | tight 66t | 0.80/0.41 | 0.52/0.15 | 0.36/0.08 |
  | **minimal 37t** | 0.77/0.52 | 0.54/0.20 | 0.36/0.08 |

  Compliance is flat; pass ties or favors the shortest. Fixed overhead per request drops from 155 to ~81 tokens (of the 1024-token input window). Prompt tokens are unmetered and prefix-cached, so the win is window room, not compute.

Smoke (4 steps, same config): no OOM at micro=2, ~750 s/step (policy_train 455 s + generate 250 s), avg generation 3,000–4,200 tokens, truncation 19–36% on the pre-RL policy (vs 40–48% at end of round 4). Pool `2026.09.02.1`: 23,265 train rows, new prompt verified in-region. Expect ~27–30 h/arm; metered spend likely 2–3× round 4.

Open questions this round answers: does the 8192 budget open grades 11–12 (round 4: budget-starved, not merely hard), and does math500 recover from the 0.656 → 0.562 regression.

issues.author: rjpower
issues.body:
The advisory lint review of #8748 surfaced structural cleanups that were deliberately not landed in that PR's final commits. Each stands alone; none changes behavior.

Rust (`lib/finelog/rust`):

- `src/store/store.rs`: `recover_claimed_table` interleaves revision arbitration, retained-spec/schema resolution, segment-to-projection-row conversion, and local rebuild plus runtime re-registration; `register_table_with` runs name/schema validation, legacy spec derivation, TableSpec cross-checks, catalog merge, engine rebuild, and the spec-lifecycle commit in one body. Split each along those seams.
- `src/maintenance/scheduler.rs`: `schedule_maintenance` repeats `schedule_flush`'s dispatch scaffold (clone limits/wake/cadence/tables, permit, run_work, clear flag, notify, undo on failed dispatch). Extract the shared scaffold.
- `src/maintenance/mod.rs`: the `Cycle::pending` bit means a different thing per work kind (migration owns the cycle, placement pending, more compaction due), and scheduler.rs stores it as `migration_pending`. Replace with an enum.
- `src/store/compaction/object_driver.rs`: `(lease, active_version, migration_backfill)` rides three signatures with the first two only forwarded; `ObjectCompaction` already travels the same path and could carry them.
- `src/store/object_store/provider.rs`: `is_object_store` is false for a local directory this module serves through an `ObjectStore`; it tests for a remote bucket URL and should be named that way.
- `src/test_support.rs`: the resolve/Proceed match scaffold repeats verbatim in `write`, `read`, `upload_staged`, `local_path`, and `compare_and_swap`, differing only in the inner call.
- `src/store/store.rs` tests: a ~25-line open/register/build-batch/write/await preamble is copy-pasted across seven tests although `write_legacy_row` and `mem_store` helpers exist, and one test outlasts a 50 ms query bound with a real 200 ms sleep instead of controlling the clock.

Python client (`lib/finelog/src/finelog/client`):

- `object_query_client.py`: `pin_catalog` does checksum-verified object loading, HEAD/catalog identity and format gating, segment URI projection, and active-spec column mapping in one body, and it navigates the HEAD/catalog documents as untyped dicts via `_mapping`/`_integer`/`_sequence` although they are proto-JSON of `CatalogHead`/`NamespaceCatalog` with generated `stats_pb2` types available.

Two review findings are recorded here as intentionally rejected so they are not re-filed: migration `0006_drop_recorded_only_columns` dropping columns that migration 0002 added, and the reserved proto field slots in `finelog_stats.proto` — the intermediate schema and fields shipped to the live marin-dev catalog, so the ordered drop-migration and reservations are required.

Done when the listed refactors land or are individually declined with a reason.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Analysis — actionable, but blocked on #8748; too large for a single PR**

**Research.** Every item here targets code introduced by [#8748](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8748) (`agent/20260827-fix-8737`), which is still **open**. On `main` five of the referenced files don't exist yet — `maintenance/mod.rs`, `maintenance/scheduler.rs`, `store/compaction/object_driver.rs`, `store/object_store/provider.rs`, and `client/object_query_client.py` are all added by that PR. The two files that do exist on `main` are in a pre-#8748 shape: `recover_claimed_table` isn't present in [`store/store.rs`](lib/finelog/rust/src/store/store.rs) yet, and `is_object_store` lives in [`store/remote.rs:37`](lib/finelog/rust/src/store/remote.rs#L37), not the `object_store/provider.rs` the issue names. I confirmed each claim against the #8748 branch: `schedule_maintenance`/`schedule_flush` (`scheduler.rs:213`/`:161`), the `pending`-poll comment (`mod.rs:21`), and `pin_catalog`'s untyped `_mapping`/`_integer`/`_sequence` navigation (`object_query_client.py:107+`).

**Why no PR now.** Two independent reasons: (1) this is a multi-module refactor (~9 items across Rust and the Python client, well over 100 lines) — larger than the single-PR bar; (2) it is blocked — landing any item on `main` is impossible (files absent) and landing on the #8748 branch pre-empts a review still in flight and guarantees rebase churn. The issue itself frames these as work "deliberately not landed in that PR's final commits," i.e. post-merge follow-ups.

**Proposed approach (for a human to green-light).** Wait for #8748 to merge, then land each item as its own small, behavior-preserving PR — they are independent by design and review cleanly in isolation. Suggested sequencing:

Rust:
1. `provider.rs` — rename `is_object_store` → a remote-bucket-URL predicate (smallest; pure rename).
2. `maintenance/mod.rs` — replace the overloaded `Cycle::pending` bit with a per-work-kind enum; update `scheduler.rs`'s `migration_pending` store.
3. `maintenance/scheduler.rs` — extract the shared dispatch scaffold between `schedule_maintenance` and `schedule_flush`.
4. `compaction/object_driver.rs` — fold `(lease, active_version, migration_backfill)` onto `ObjectCompaction` instead of threading them through three signatures.
5. `test_support.rs` — collapse the repeated resolve/`Proceed` match in `write`/`read`/`upload_staged`/`local_path`/`compare_and_swap`.
6. `store/store.rs` — split `recover_claimed_table` and `register_table_with` along their seams; dedup the seven copy-pasted test preambles via the existing `write_legacy_row`/`mem_store` helpers and replace the real 200 ms sleep with a controlled clock.

Python:
7. `object_query_client.py` — split `pin_catalog`'s concerns and parse HEAD/catalog as the generated `CatalogHead`/`NamespaceCatalog`/`stats_pb2` protos instead of untyped dicts.

Each PR should carry a regression-safe test only where behavior boundaries actually move (enum swap, `pin_catalog` split); the pure renames and scaffold extractions need none beyond the existing suite. The two rejected findings (migration `0006` drop ordering, reserved `finelog_stats.proto` slots) are correctly recorded as declined and need no action.

I've left this unimplemented pending #8748 and a maintainer's go-ahead on the plan above. Happy to pick up any single item as its own PR once #8748 lands.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
## Human Authored tl;dr

WHAT THIS IS: A five-model MoE panel evaluated on every source in tasktrove 3.42 (~300 samples per cell).
WHY WE DID IT: Uncover data quality issues in TaskTrove, better understand the relationship between model capacity and agentic benchmark performance, understand whether TaskTrove sources tend to covary or reveal significant gaps in coverage between the MoEs.
RESULT: Several data quality issues in TaskTrove were found and mitigated; see TaskTrove readme on HF for details. Further data quality issues were observed but not yet mitigated; will be addressed in future TaskTrove updates. Despite this, many sources in TaskTrove now exhibit the desirably property; significant delta between models that tends to covary with subjective perceptions of model quality. The diversity of TaskTrove helps to reveal gaps in post-training (e.g. SWE tasks and Java coding for Gemma-4 MoE). The data also clearly indicates that model capacity is *not* predictive of agentic benchmark performance; recent small MoEs regularly match and sometimes even outperform GLM 5.2.

## Artifacts

- [Interactive five-model reward report](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/penfever/tasktrove-v342-five-model-reward/2026.08.23/index.html)
- [Experiment archive](https://huggingface.co/datasets/penfever/moe-data-quality)
